Chapter 1: Growing Up Cut Off from the World
Imagine your childhood unfolding far from the usual sounds of school bells or the laughter of neighborhood kids. Picture a remote Idaho valley, where one family is building a life right on the edge of society—driven by a belief that everything outside their world is dangerous and corrupt.
Out here, days are shaped by the rhythm of the land, the changing seasons, and above all, the strict rules of a father who trusts no one but himself. For the children, their world is tiny—it’s just the mountain, the family’s battered house, and a junkyard that doubles as both playground and workplace.
School isn’t a given here. In fact, formal education is seen as a threat—not a right. The kids are expected to work. They help run the family’s scrap business, and every task is meant to prepare them for a future their father warns them may never come. His voice is always there, reminding them about government intrusion and the looming end times, shaping every single decision they make.
Their mother? She’s caught in the middle—torn between her husband’s fierce convictions and her own quiet doubts. Sometimes, she keeps the family together with herbal remedies pulled from the land. Other times, she bends the rules just enough to keep them afloat.
One of the youngest children—a girl with a sharp mind and a restless spirit—spends her days watching her older siblings. Some break away, heading off to college or jobs. Others stay, trapped in the family’s orbit. She fills her days sorting metal, helping bottle herbs, and listening to her father’s endless stories about dangers lurking just beyond their mountain. The outside world is a mystery to her—something she glimpses only during rare trips to town or in the battered textbooks gathering dust on the shelf.
Most of us grow up taking simple routines for granted—school, friendships, teachers who are always there. But not in this family. Here, learning comes in fits and starts, if it happens at all. The children are taught to distrust outsiders, to rely only on themselves, and to accept pain as just another part of life. Injuries from the junkyard happen all the time, but hospitals? They’re strictly off-limits. The only medicine allowed is whatever their mother can whip up at home.
As the years pass, the girl starts to notice the cracks in her world. She sees how her father’s fears dictate every choice, how her mother’s quiet strength keeps everyone going, and how her siblings struggle to forge their own paths. The boundaries of her life feel both safe and confining. There’s a longing—a sense that another life might be possible, if only she could figure out how to reach it.
For this family, isolation is both a shield and a prison. Sure, it keeps out the dangers her father dreads, but it also blocks out opportunity, connection, and growth. The girl’s early years are filled with this constant tension—torn between loyalty to her family and a growing curiosity about what’s out there beyond the mountain. And it’s this tension that will shape every step of her journey, as she dares to imagine a future her parents never planned for her.
